claim: BECs undergo rapid activation into proliferating progenitors during severe or chronic hepatic injury, which is a crucial step required to establish a regenerative process known as ductular reaction (DR).
source: During severe or chronic hepatic injury, biliary epithelial cells (BECs) undergo rapid activation into proliferating progenitors, a crucial step required to establish a regenerative process known as ductular reaction (DR).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript.

claim: DR is a hallmark of chronic liver diseases, including advanced stages of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
source: While DR is a hallmark of chronic liver diseases, including advanced stages of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), the early events underlying BEC activation are largely unknown.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: BECs readily accumulate lipids during high-fat diet feeding in mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that BECs readily accumulate lipids during high-fat diet feeding in mice and upon fatty acid treatment in BEC-derived organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H-I and related text.

claim: BECs readily accumulate lipids upon fatty acid treatment in BEC-derived organoids.
source: Here, we demonstrate that BECs readily accumulate lipids during high-fat diet feeding in mice and upon fatty acid treatment in BEC-derived organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and related text.

claim: Lipid overload induces metabolic rewiring to support the conversion of adult cholangiocytes into reactive BECs.
source: Lipid overload induces metabolic rewiring to support the conversion of adult cholangiocytes into reactive BECs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including gene expression changes (Figure 1E-F) and metabolic assays (Figure 4).

claim: Lipid overload activates the E2F transcription factors in BECs.
source: Mechanistically, we found that lipid overload activates the E2F transcription factors in BECs, which drive cell cycle progression while promoting glycolytic metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis (Figure 3B-C) and functional studies (Figure 3E-F).

claim: E2F transcription factors drive cell cycle progression in BECs.
source: Mechanistically, we found that lipid overload activates the E2F transcription factors in BECs, which drive cell cycle progression while promoting glycolytic metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing E2F inhibition reduces proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and E2f1 knockout prevents BEC activation (Figure 3E-F).

claim: E2F transcription factors promote glycolytic metabolism in BECs.
source: Mechanistically, we found that lipid overload activates the E2F transcription factors in BECs, which drive cell cycle progression while promoting glycolytic metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing E2F inhibition reduces glycolysis (Figure 4H-K) and gene expression changes (Figure 4G).

claim: Fat overload is sufficient to reprogram BECs into progenitor cells in the early stages of NAFLD.
source: These findings demonstrate that fat overload is sufficient to reprogram BECs into progenitor cells in the early stages of NAFLD and provide new insights into the mechanistic basis of this process, revealing unexpected connections between lipid metabolism, stemness, and regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased proliferation (Figure 2C-G) and organoid formation capacity (Figure 2I) in HFD-fed mice.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the hepatic epithelium, composed of hepatocytes and BECs (or cholangiocytes), is non-proliferative.
source: Under physiological conditions, the hepatic epithelium, composed of hepatocytes and BECs (or cholangiocytes), is non-proliferative.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Upon injury, hepatocytes and BECs are capable of rapidly changing their phenotype from quiescent to proliferative, contributing to the prompt restoration of damaged tissue.
source: Yet upon injury, these two cell types are capable of rapidly changing their phenotype from quiescent to proliferative, contributing to the prompt restoration of damaged tissue (Gadd et al., 2020; Michalopoulos, 2014; Miyajima et al., 2014; Yanger and Stanger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In chronic liver injury, characterized by impaired hepatocyte replication, BECs serve as the cell source for regenerative cellular expansion through the DR process.
source: However, in chronic liver injury, characterized by impaired hepatocyte replication, BECs weigh-in and serve as the cell source for regenerative cellular expansion through the DR process (Choi et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2018; Español-Suñer et al., 2012; Huch et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2015; Raven et al., 2017; Rodrigo-Torres et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Several signaling pathways involving YAP have been reported to drive the DR process in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using DDC.
source: The molecular basis by which BECs expand during the DR has been extensively studied in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using the chemical 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC). Several signaling pathways involving YAP (Meyer et al., 2020; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019), mTORC1 (Planas-Paz et al., 2019), TET1-mediated hydroxymethylation (Aloia et al., 2019) and NCAM1 (Tsuchiya et al., 2014) have been reported to drive this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several signaling pathways involving mTORC1 have been reported to drive the DR process in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using DDC.
source: The molecular basis by which BECs expand during the DR has been extensively studied in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using the chemical 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC). Several signaling pathways involving YAP (Meyer et al., 2020; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019), mTORC1 (Planas-Paz et al., 2019), TET1-mediated hydroxymethylation (Aloia et al., 2019) and NCAM1 (Tsuchiya et al., 2014) have been reported to drive this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several signaling pathways involving TET1-mediated hydroxymethylation have been reported to drive the DR process in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using DDC.
source: The molecular basis by which BECs expand during the DR has been extensively studied in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using the chemical 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC). Several signaling pathways involving YAP (Meyer et al., 2020; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019), mTORC1 (Planas-Paz et al., 2019), TET1-mediated hydroxymethylation (Aloia et al., 2019) and NCAM1 (Tsuchiya et al., 2014) have been reported to drive this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several signaling pathways involving NCAM1 have been reported to drive the DR process in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using DDC.
source: The molecular basis by which BECs expand during the DR has been extensively studied in models of chemical biliary damage and portal fibrosis using the chemical 3,5-diethoxycarbonyl-1,4-dihydrocollidine (DDC). Several signaling pathways involving YAP (Meyer et al., 2020; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019), mTORC1 (Planas-Paz et al., 2019), TET1-mediated hydroxymethylation (Aloia et al., 2019) and NCAM1 (Tsuchiya et al., 2014) have been reported to drive this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DR has been observed in late-stage NAFLD patients with fibrosis and portal inflammation.
source: Importantly, DR has also been observed in late-stage NAFLD patients with fibrosis and portal inflammation (Gadd et al., 2014; Sato et al., 2019; Sorrentino et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NAFLD is one of the most common chronic diseases.
source: NAFLD, one of the most common chronic diseases, initiates with increased lipid accumulation, a stage called steatosis (Paschos and Paletas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: NAFLD initiates with increased lipid accumulation, a stage called steatosis.
source: NAFLD, one of the most common chronic diseases, initiates with increased lipid accumulation, a stage called steatosis (Paschos and Paletas, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: NAFLD progresses into inflammation and fibrosis that can cause cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: This pathology progresses into inflammation and fibrosis that can cause cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, which are the most frequent liver transplantation indications (Byrne and Targher, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma are the most frequent liver transplantation indications.
source: This pathology progresses into inflammation and fibrosis that can cause cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, which are the most frequent liver transplantation indications (Byrne and Targher, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: YAP has been found to be activated in BECs in fibrotic livers but not in steatosis.
source: YAP has been found to be activated in BECs in fibrotic livers but not in steatosis (Machado et al., 2015), suggesting that YAP activation is necessary to support DR in the late fibrotic NAFLD stages, and thus, leaving the early molecular mechanisms of BEC activation, which precede the onset of the DR, unexplored.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: YAP activation is necessary to support DR in the late fibrotic NAFLD stages.
source: YAP has been found to be activated in BECs in fibrotic livers but not in steatosis (Machado et al., 2015), suggesting that YAP activation is necessary to support DR in the late fibrotic NAFLD stages, and thus, leaving the early molecular mechanisms of BEC activation, which precede the onset of the DR, unexplored.
evidence: This claim is presented as an inference from the cited literature.

claim: BEC-derived organoids can be established from intrahepatic bile duct progenitors and can proliferate.
source: BEC-derived organoids (BEC-organoids) can be established from intrahepatic bile duct progenitors and can proliferate, representing a promising in vitro approach to study regenerative mechanisms and therapies (Huch et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017; Okabe et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2011; Sorrentino et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC-organoids represent a promising in vitro approach to study regenerative mechanisms and therapies.
source: BEC-derived organoids (BEC-organoids) can be established from intrahepatic bile duct progenitors and can proliferate, representing a promising in vitro approach to study regenerative mechanisms and therapies (Huch et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017; Okabe et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2011; Sorrentino et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC-organoids are self-renewing bi-potent organoids that express biliary progenitor markers.
source: These self-renewing bi-potent organoids express biliary progenitor markers and are capable of differentiating into functional cholangiocyte- and hepatocyte-like lineages in specific differentiation media, which can engraft and repair bile ducts (Hallett et al., 2022; Sampaziotis et al., 2021) and improve liver function when transplanted into a mouse with liver disease (Huch et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC-organoids are capable of differentiating into functional cholangiocyte- and hepatocyte-like lineages in specific differentiation media.
source: These self-renewing bi-potent organoids express biliary progenitor markers and are capable of differentiating into functional cholangiocyte- and hepatocyte-like lineages in specific differentiation media, which can engraft and repair bile ducts (Hallett et al., 2022; Sampaziotis et al., 2021) and improve liver function when transplanted into a mouse with liver disease (Huch et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC-organoids can engraft and repair bile ducts.
source: These self-renewing bi-potent organoids express biliary progenitor markers and are capable of differentiating into functional cholangiocyte- and hepatocyte-like lineages in specific differentiation media, which can engraft and repair bile ducts (Hallett et al., 2022; Sampaziotis et al., 2021) and improve liver function when transplanted into a mouse with liver disease (Huch et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC-organoids improve liver function when transplanted into a mouse with liver disease.
source: These self-renewing bi-potent organoids express biliary progenitor markers and are capable of differentiating into functional cholangiocyte- and hepatocyte-like lineages in specific differentiation media, which can engraft and repair bile ducts (Hallett et al., 2022; Sampaziotis et al., 2021) and improve liver function when transplanted into a mouse with liver disease (Huch et al., 2015; Huch et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC-organoids efficiently accumulated lipid droplets in a dose-dependent manner when treated with a mixture of oleic acid and palmitic acid.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that BEC-organoids efficiently accumulated lipid droplets in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1B), and this process did not affect organoid viability (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lipid accumulation in BEC-organoids did not affect organoid viability.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that BEC-organoids efficiently accumulated lipid droplets in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1B), and this process did not affect organoid viability (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Oleic acid and palmitic acid are the two most abundant FAs found in livers of NAFLD patients.
source: To gain insight into how chronic lipid exposure, which induces liver steatosis, affects biliary progenitor function in vitro, we incubated single BECs with a mixture of oleic acid (OA) and palmitic acid (PA) (the fatty acid (FA) mix) – the two most abundant FAs found in livers of NAFLD patients (Araya et al., 2004), for 7 days and allowed BEC-organoid formation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: FA addition affected the expression of Scd1 in BEC-organoids.
source: To investigate how cells adapt their metabolism to lipid overload, we monitored the expression of several genes involved in lipid metabolism, including Scd1 (de novo lipogenesis) (Figure 1E), Hmgcs2 (ketogenesis), Pdk4 (inhibition of pyruvate oxidation), and Aldh1a1 (prevention against lipid peroxidation products) (Figure 1F) and found it to be affected by FA addition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FA addition affected the expression of Hmgcs2 in BEC-organoids.
source: To investigate how cells adapt their metabolism to lipid overload, we monitored the expression of several genes involved in lipid metabolism, including Scd1 (de novo lipogenesis) (Figure 1E), Hmgcs2 (ketogenesis), Pdk4 (inhibition of pyruvate oxidation), and Aldh1a1 (prevention against lipid peroxidation products) (Figure 1F) and found it to be affected by FA addition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FA addition affected the expression of Pdk4 in BEC-organoids.
source: To investigate how cells adapt their metabolism to lipid overload, we monitored the expression of several genes involved in lipid metabolism, including Scd1 (de novo lipogenesis) (Figure 1E), Hmgcs2 (ketogenesis), Pdk4 (inhibition of pyruvate oxidation), and Aldh1a1 (prevention against lipid peroxidation products) (Figure 1F) and found it to be affected by FA addition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FA addition affected the expression of Aldh1a1 in BEC-organoids.
source: To investigate how cells adapt their metabolism to lipid overload, we monitored the expression of several genes involved in lipid metabolism, including Scd1 (de novo lipogenesis) (Figure 1E), Hmgcs2 (ketogenesis), Pdk4 (inhibition of pyruvate oxidation), and Aldh1a1 (prevention against lipid peroxidation products) (Figure 1F) and found it to be affected by FA addition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: BEC organoids actively reprogram their metabolism to cope with aberrant lipid overload.
source: These results suggest that BEC organoids actively reprogram their metabolism to cope with aberrant lipid overload.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the gene expression changes observed in Figure 1E-F.

claim: HFD-fed mice gained weight and developed liver steatosis, but no apparent fibrosis.
source: As expected, HFD-fed mice gained weight and developed liver steatosis, but no apparent fibrosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HFD-feeding led to an accumulation of lipid droplets in the periportal zone.
source: Of note, HFD-feeding led to an accumulation of lipid droplets in the periportal zone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and within bile ducts, as reflected by the localization of BODIPY signal in PANCK (BEC marker) positive cells (Figure 1H), without inducing epithelial damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: HFD-feeding led to an accumulation of lipid droplets within bile ducts.
source: Of note, HFD-feeding led to an accumulation of lipid droplets in the periportal zone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and within bile ducts, as reflected by the localization of BODIPY signal in PANCK (BEC marker) positive cells (Figure 1H), without inducing epithelial damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: HFD-feeding did not induce epithelial damage in bile ducts.
source: Of note, HFD-feeding led to an accumulation of lipid droplets in the periportal zone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and within bile ducts, as reflected by the localization of BODIPY signal in PANCK (BEC marker) positive cells (Figure 1H), without inducing epithelial damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis of BECs stained with EPCAM and BODIPY confirmed that BECs are able to store lipids upon HFD feeding.
source: Moreover, flow cytometry analysis of BECs stained with EPCAM, a pan-BEC marker (Aloia et al., 2019; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019) and BODIPY confirmed that these cells are able to store lipids upon HFD feeding (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L.

claim: EPCAM is a pan-BEC marker.
source: Moreover, flow cytometry analysis of BECs stained with EPCAM, a pan-BEC marker (Aloia et al., 2019; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019) and BODIPY confirmed that these cells are able to store lipids upon HFD feeding (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HFD feeding induces considerable transcriptional changes in BECs in vivo.
source: Analysis of these data revealed a diet-dependent clustering in Principal Component Analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that HFD feeding induces considerable transcriptional changes in BECs in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Differential expression analysis revealed a total of 495 significantly changed genes in BECs upon HFD feeding, with 121 upregulated and 374 downregulated.
source: Differential expression analysis further revealed a total of 495 significantly changed genes, 121 upregulated and 374 downregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HFD promoted the upregulation of Ncam1 in BECs.
source: At the same time, HFD promoted the upregulation of Ncam1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), a well-established mediator of BEC activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ncam1 is a well-established mediator of BEC activation.
source: At the same time, HFD promoted the upregulation of Ncam1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), a well-established mediator of BEC activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Canonical markers of the DR were not changed in EPCAM+ BECs isolated from livers of HFD-fed mice.
source: Consistent with the absence of fibrosis and biliary epithelial damage, canonical makers of the DR (Manco et al., 2019; Sato et al., 2019; Tsuchiya et al., 2014) were not changed in EPCAM+ BECs isolated from livers of HFD-fed mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Cell proliferation is the major process induced in BECs upon HFD feeding.
source: To further explore the transcriptional changes, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on Gene Ontology (GO) terms (Figure 2B) and KEGG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) pathways and identified cell proliferation, the most prevalent early feature of BEC activation (Sato et al., 2019) as the major process induced in these cells upon HFD feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cell proliferation is the most prevalent early feature of BEC activation.
source: To further explore the transcriptional changes, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on Gene Ontology (GO) terms (Figure 2B) and KEGG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) pathways and identified cell proliferation, the most prevalent early feature of BEC activation (Sato et al., 2019) as the major process induced in these cells upon HFD feeding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expansion of reactive BECs requires detachment from their niche and invasion of the parenchyma toward the damaged hepatic area.
source: Expansion of the reactive BECs requires detachment from their niche and invasion of the parenchyma toward the damaged hepatic area.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Reorganizing the extracellular matrix (ECM) and reducing focal adhesion are processes that make possible the expansion of reactive BECs.
source: This process is made possible by reorganizing the extracellular matrix (ECM) and reducing focal adhesion, effectively downregulated in EPCAM+ BECs upon HFD (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ECM organization and focal adhesion pathways are effectively downregulated in EPCAM+ BECs upon HFD.
source: This process is made possible by reorganizing the extracellular matrix (ECM) and reducing focal adhesion, effectively downregulated in EPCAM+ BECs upon HFD (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: HFD feeding was sufficient to induce a marked increase in the number of active BECs (Ki67+/OPN+ cells).
source: Of note, we found that HFD feeding was sufficient to induce a marked increase in the number of active BECs (i.e. Ki67+/OPN+ cells- Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Chronic lipid exposure stimulates the appearance of reactive BECs within the bile ducts.
source: Similar results were observed in two independent cohorts of mice challenged with HFD and injected with EdU either to track proliferating cells by immunofluorescence (Figure 2E–F) or to quantify by flow cytometry the amount of EPCAM+/EdU+ BECs in the liver (Figure 2G), confirming that chronic lipid exposure stimulates the appearance of reactive BECs within the bile ducts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The efficiency of BECs to generate organoids in vitro mirrors their activation status.
source: The efficiency of BECs to generate organoids in vitro has been shown to mirror their activation status (Aloia et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HFD-derived BECs were significantly more efficient in generating organoids than their CD counterparts.
source: Strikingly, we observed that HFD-derived BECs were significantly more efficient in generating organoids than their CD counterparts (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: HFD feeding is sufficient to induce, in vivo, the exit of BECs from a quiescent state and the acquisition of both proliferative and pro-regenerative features.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that HFD feeding is sufficient to induce, in vivo, the exit of BECs from a quiescent state and the acquisition of both proliferative and pro-regenerative features.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cell division, mitosis, and chromosome segregation were the shared enriched pathways for upregulated genes in HFD and DDC samples.
source: We identified the most pronounced changes shared between HFD and DDC samples by overlapping separate over-representation enrichment analyses (Supplementary file 2). Cell division, mitosis, and chromosome segregation were the shared enriched pathways for upregulated genes in HFD and DDC samples (Figure 3A), while ECM organization was the shared enriched pathway for the downregulated genes in HFD and DDC conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by over-representation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ECM organization was the shared enriched pathway for the downregulated genes in HFD and DDC conditions.
source: We identified the most pronounced changes shared between HFD and DDC samples by overlapping separate over-representation enrichment analyses (Supplementary file 2). Cell division, mitosis, and chromosome segregation were the shared enriched pathways for upregulated genes in HFD and DDC samples (Figure 3A), while ECM organization was the shared enriched pathway for the downregulated genes in HFD and DDC conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by over-representation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mechanisms of BEC activation induced by lipid overload partially overlap with those by which BECs expand during the DR with biliary epithelial damage.
source: We concluded that the mechanisms of BEC activation induced by lipid overload partially overlap with those by which BECs expand during the DR with biliary epithelial damage.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparison of HFD and DDC transcriptional profiles.

claim: A more detailed analysis of DDC- and HFD-derived BECs revealed the concomitant enrichment of four overlapping transcription factor (TF) gene sets, E2F1-4.
source: Of note, a more detailed analysis of DDC- and HFD-derived BECs, revealed the concomitant enrichment of four overlapping transcription factor (TF) gene sets, E2F1-4 (Figure 3B), and their target genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which have not been linked to BEC activation or DR previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: E2F1-4 have not been linked to BEC activation or DR previously.
source: Of note, a more detailed analysis of DDC- and HFD-derived BECs, revealed the concomitant enrichment of four overlapping transcription factor (TF) gene sets, E2F1-4 (Figure 3B), and their target genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which have not been linked to BEC activation or DR previously.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: E2Fs and cell division pathway are the most upregulated genes in proliferating BEC-organoids.
source: Moreover, we identified an enrichment of E2Fs (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 2) and cell division pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) as the most upregulated genes in proliferating BEC-organoids, further corroborating the role of E2Fs in these two in vitro (Aloia et al., 2019) and in vivo (Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019) DR models.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: E2Fs are a large family of TFs with complex functions in cell cycle progression, DNA replication, repair, and G2/M checkpoints.
source: E2Fs are a large family of TFs with complex functions in cell cycle progression, DNA replication, repair, and G2/M checkpoints (Dimova and Dyson, 2005; Dyson, 1998; Dyson, 2016; Ren et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activation of E2Fs represents an early event in the process of BEC activation, which is necessary for exiting the quiescent state and promoting BEC expansion.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the activation of E2Fs might represent an early event in the process of BEC activation, which is necessary for exiting the quiescent state and promoting BEC expansion.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the data and knowledge of E2F function.

claim: E2f1-/- mice were refractory to BEC activation induced by lipid overload upon HFD, as opposed to E2f1+/+ mice.
source: Remarkably, E2f1-/- mice were refractory to BEC activation induced by lipid overload upon HFD, as opposed to E2f1+/+ mice (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Silencing of E2F1 in EPCAM+ BECs from livers of C57BL/6 J HFD-fed mice reduced the capacity to form organoids in vitro.
source: In addition, silencing of E2F1 in EPCAM+ BECs from livers of C57BL/6 J HFD-fed mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) reduced the capacity to form organoids in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: E2F1 plays a previously unrecognized role in controlling BEC activation during HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in vivo.
source: These results demonstrate a previously unrecognized role of E2F1 in controlling BEC activation during HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in vivo and support a pivotal role of this transcription factor in controlling BEC expansion.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: E2F1 plays a pivotal role in controlling BEC expansion.
source: These results demonstrate a previously unrecognized role of E2F1 in controlling BEC activation during HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in vivo and support a pivotal role of this transcription factor in controlling BEC expansion.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 3.

claim: The exit of terminally-differentiated cells from their quiescent state requires both energy and building block availability to support cell proliferation.
source: The exit of terminally-differentiated cells from their quiescent state requires both energy and building block availability to support cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Proliferative cells reprogram their glucose metabolism to meet their increased need for biomass and energy.
source: Proliferative cells, therefore, reprogram their glucose metabolism to meet their increased need for biomass and energy (Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Purine and pyrimidine metabolism, as well as the pentose-phosphate pathway, are enriched during in vitro BEC-organoid formation.
source: Supporting this notion, our interrogation of in vitro BEC-organoid formation dataset (Aloia et al., 2019) revealed the enrichment of purine and pyrimidine metabolism, as well as the pentose-phosphate pathway, which is tightly connected to glycolysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The pentose-phosphate pathway is tightly connected to glycolysis.
source: Supporting this notion, our interrogation of in vitro BEC-organoid formation dataset (Aloia et al., 2019) revealed the enrichment of purine and pyrimidine metabolism, as well as the pentose-phosphate pathway, which is tightly connected to glycolysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: A substrate oxidation test in BEC-organoids revealed a preference for glucose, as reflected by the decrease in maximal respiration when UK5099, a mitochondrial pyruvate carrier inhibitor, was used.
source: In line with these findings, a substrate oxidation test in BEC-organoids revealed a preference for glucose, as reflected by the decrease in maximal respiration, when UK5099, a mitochondrial pyruvate carrier inhibitor, was used (Figure 4A–B), while no changes were observed with inhibitors of glutamine (BPTES) and FA (Etomoxir) metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: No changes in maximal respiration were observed with inhibitors of glutamine (BPTES) and FA (Etomoxir) metabolism in BEC-organoids.
source: In line with these findings, a substrate oxidation test in BEC-organoids revealed a preference for glucose, as reflected by the decrease in maximal respiration, when UK5099, a mitochondrial pyruvate carrier inhibitor, was used (Figure 4A–B), while no changes were observed with inhibitors of glutamine (BPTES) and FA (Etomoxir) metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: HFD-FA BEC-organoids demonstrated increased compensatory glycolytic rates.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, HFD-FA BEC-organoids demonstrated increased compensatory glycolytic rates (Figure 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: There was a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in HFD-FA BEC-organoids, as evidenced by the decrease in maximal respiration.
source: Of note, there was a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in HFD-FA BEC-organoids, as evidenced by the decrease in maximal respiration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G), which might reflect their preference for the glycolytic pathway to generate biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: The decrease in maximal respiration in HFD-FA BEC-organoids might reflect their preference for the glycolytic pathway to generate biomass.
source: Of note, there was a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in HFD-FA BEC-organoids, as evidenced by the decrease in maximal respiration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G), which might reflect their preference for the glycolytic pathway to generate biomass.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: E2Fs coordinate several aspects of cellular metabolism.
source: Besides their prominent role in cell cycle progression, E2Fs coordinate several aspects of cellular metabolism (Denechaud et al., 2017; Nicolay and Dyson, 2013), and promote glycolysis in different contexts (Blanchet et al., 2011; Denechaud et al., 2016; Huber et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: E2Fs promote glycolysis in different contexts.
source: Besides their prominent role in cell cycle progression, E2Fs coordinate several aspects of cellular metabolism (Denechaud et al., 2017; Nicolay and Dyson, 2013), and promote glycolysis in different contexts (Blanchet et al., 2011; Denechaud et al., 2016; Huber et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HLM006474 treatment reduced the transcriptional levels of several genes involved in cell cycle progression and glycolytic metabolism in BEC-organoids.
source: As expected, HLM006474 treatment reduced the transcriptional levels of several genes involved in cell cycle progression and glycolytic metabolism (Figure 4G) and decreased the glycolytic flux, as evidenced by the blunted proton efflux rate (PER) (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: HLM006474 treatment decreased the glycolytic flux in BEC-organoids, as evidenced by the blunted proton efflux rate (PER).
source: As expected, HLM006474 treatment reduced the transcriptional levels of several genes involved in cell cycle progression and glycolytic metabolism (Figure 4G) and decreased the glycolytic flux, as evidenced by the blunted proton efflux rate (PER) (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: E2F inhibition was able to reverse the metabolic phenotype only in HFD-FA BEC-organoids.
source: Moreover, E2F inhibition was able to reverse the metabolic phenotype only in HFD-FA BEC-organoids (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: HFD-induced E2F activation controls the conversion of BECs from quiescent to active progenitors by promoting the expression of cell cycle genes while simultaneously driving a shift toward glycolysis.
source: In conclusion, these results demonstrate that HFD-induced E2F activation controls the conversion of BECs from quiescent to active progenitors by promoting the expression of cell cycle genes while simultaneously driving a shift toward glycolysis.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Through DR activation, BECs represent an essential reservoir of progenitors that are crucial for coordinating hepatic epithelial regeneration in the context of chronic liver diseases.
source: Through DR activation, BECs represent an essential reservoir of progenitors that are crucial for coordinating hepatic epithelial regeneration in the context of chronic liver diseases (Choi et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2018; Español-Suñer et al., 2012; Huch et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2015; Raven et al., 2017; Rodrigo-Torres et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BEC functions are tightly controlled by YAP metabolic pathways.
source: BEC functions are tightly controlled by YAP metabolic pathways (Meyer et al., 2020; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019), and recent studies from different tissues have provided evidence that specific metabolic states play instructive roles in controlling cell fate and tissue regeneration (Beyaz et al., 2016; Capolupo et al., 2022; Miao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Specific metabolic states play instructive roles in controlling cell fate and tissue regeneration.
source: BEC functions are tightly controlled by YAP metabolic pathways (Meyer et al., 2020; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019; Planas-Paz et al., 2019), and recent studies from different tissues have provided evidence that specific metabolic states play instructive roles in controlling cell fate and tissue regeneration (Beyaz et al., 2016; Capolupo et al., 2022; Miao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Aberrant lipid accumulation is a hallmark of early NAFLD.
source: Aberrant lipid accumulation is a hallmark of early NAFLD, and imbalances in lipid metabolism are known to affect hepatocyte homeostasis, including induction of lipo-toxicity and cell death (Wang et al., 2016b; Sano et al., 2021; De Gottardi et al., 2007; Wobser et al., 2009; Ipsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Imbalances in lipid metabolism are known to affect hepatocyte homeostasis, including induction of lipo-toxicity and cell death.
source: Aberrant lipid accumulation is a hallmark of early NAFLD, and imbalances in lipid metabolism are known to affect hepatocyte homeostasis, including induction of lipo-toxicity and cell death (Wang et al., 2016b; Sano et al., 2021; De Gottardi et al., 2007; Wobser et al., 2009; Ipsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: BECs are resistant to lipid-induced toxicity.
source: Here, using HFD- fed mouse models, we studied BEC metabolism in steatosis, the first stage of NAFLD, and demonstrated lipid accumulation in BECs during chronic HFD in vivo and their resistance to lipid-induced toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no effect on viability (Figure 1C-D) and no epithelial damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-I).

claim: FAs directly target BECs, without any involvement of hepatocytes.
source: By using BEC-organoids, we observed that FAs directly target BECs, without any involvement of hepatocytes and that BECs functionally respond to lipid overload.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the use of isolated BEC-organoids which do not contain hepatocytes.

claim: BECs functionally respond to lipid overload.
source: By using BEC-organoids, we observed that FAs directly target BECs, without any involvement of hepatocytes and that BECs functionally respond to lipid overload.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing metabolic changes (Figure 1E-F, Figure 4).

claim: BEC-organoids derived from CD- and HFD-fed mouse livers shift their cellular metabolism toward more glycolysis in the presence of lipids.
source: Importantly, BEC-organoids derived from CD- and HFD-fed mouse livers were shown to shift their cellular metabolism toward more glycolysis in the presence of lipids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The HFD-induced metabolic shift was sufficient to reprogram BEC identity in vivo, allowing their exit from a quiescent state and the simultaneous acquisition of progenitor functions, such as proliferation and organoid-initiating capacity.
source: Furthermore, we found that the HFD-induced metabolic shift was sufficient to reprogram BEC identity in vivo, allowing their exit from a quiescent state and the simultaneous acquisition of progenitor functions, such as proliferation and organoid-initiating capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lipid overload is sufficient to induce BEC activation in steatotic livers and this process precedes parenchymal damage.
source: Importantly, we observed that lipid overload is sufficient to induce BEC activation in steatotic livers and that this process precedes parenchymal damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing BEC activation without fibrosis or epithelial damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, G-I, Figure 2).

claim: Long-term feeding of a lipid-enriched diet strongly promotes BEC proliferation.
source: To fully understand the underlying basis of the observed phenotype, we characterized the transcriptome of primary BECs derived from steatotic livers of HFD-fed mice and demonstrated that long-term feeding of a lipid-enriched diet strongly promotes BEC proliferation, suggesting a strong link between metabolic adaptation and progenitor function.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a strong link between metabolic adaptation and progenitor function in BECs.
source: To fully understand the underlying basis of the observed phenotype, we characterized the transcriptome of primary BECs derived from steatotic livers of HFD-fed mice and demonstrated that long-term feeding of a lipid-enriched diet strongly promotes BEC proliferation, suggesting a strong link between metabolic adaptation and progenitor function.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: E2F transcription factors are master regulators of BEC activation in the context of NAFLD.
source: By combining our transcriptomic analysis with data mining of publicly available DR datasets (Aloia et al., 2019; Pepe-Mooney et al., 2019), we identified the E2F transcription factors as master regulators of BEC activation in the context of NAFLD.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis (Figure 3) and functional studies (Figure 3E-F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E).

claim: The expression of Pdk4, an E2F1 target, was upregulated in FA-treated BEC-organoids and upon HFD.
source: Moreover, the expression of Pdk4, an E2F1 target (Hsieh et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2016a), was upregulated in FA-treated BEC-organoids and upon HFD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Pdk4 is an E2F1 target.
source: Moreover, the expression of Pdk4, an E2F1 target (Hsieh et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2016a), was upregulated in FA-treated BEC-organoids and upon HFD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PDK4 limits the utilization of pyruvate for oxidative metabolism while enhancing glycolysis.
source: PDK4 limits the utilization of pyruvate for oxidative metabolism while enhancing glycolysis, which reinforces our data demonstrating that E2Fs rewire BEC metabolism toward glycolysis to fuel progenitor proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: E2Fs rewire BEC metabolism toward glycolysis to fuel progenitor proliferation.
source: PDK4 limits the utilization of pyruvate for oxidative metabolism while enhancing glycolysis, which reinforces our data demonstrating that E2Fs rewire BEC metabolism toward glycolysis to fuel progenitor proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: E2Fs are the molecular rheostat integrating the metabolic cell state with the cell cycle machinery to coordinate BEC activation.
source: These observations feature E2Fs as the molecular rheostat integrating the metabolic cell state with the cell cycle machinery to coordinate BEC activation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: A recent report showed increased numbers of cholangiocytes in steatotic human livers.
source: While our data are derived from obese mice, a recent report showed increased numbers of cholangiocytes in steatotic human livers (Hallett et al., 2022), and E2F1 has been found to be upregulated in the livers of obese patients (Denechaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: E2F1 has been found to be upregulated in the livers of obese patients.
source: While our data are derived from obese mice, a recent report showed increased numbers of cholangiocytes in steatotic human livers (Hallett et al., 2022), and E2F1 has been found to be upregulated in the livers of obese patients (Denechaud et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Human subjects with elevated visceral fat demonstrated increased glucose metabolism.
source: Moreover, human subjects with elevated visceral fat demonstrated increased glucose metabolism (Broadfield et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.
